planting.note: Plant offsets or nursery divisions in spring in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun to bright light; hedgehog aloe is a compact South African species suited to rock gardens, troughs, and containers.

directions: Plant in gritty, sharply draining soil in full sun to light shade, choosing a spot protected from prolonged winter wet. Dense, low rosettes of thick, blue-gray leaves are covered in small, raised, pale tubercles that give the foliage a distinctively bumpy, spiny-looking texture, and the clumping habit quickly forms an expanding mat as offsets crowd around the parent rosette. Coral-orange tubular flowers rise on slender spikes above the foliage in late winter to spring, drawing sunbirds and hummingbirds where hardy. Water sparingly and only during active growth, letting the soil dry fully between waterings, and divide congested clumps every few years to keep the display tidy.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Tiger Tooth Aloe (Tiger Tooth Miniature Aloe)

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring in fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to bright light; tiger tooth aloe is frost-tender and best grown as a container or houseplant specimen outside zones 10-11.

directions: Grow in fast-draining, gritty soil in full sun to bright light, giving some afternoon shade in the hottest inland climates to prevent scorch. Short, stacked, triangular leaves densely toothed along both margins spiral upward from freely branching stems that readily topple and root where they touch soil, so the plant quickly forms a spreading, self-layering colony. Bright red-orange sun exposure intensifies the leaf color from green toward bronze, while shaded plants stay a softer green. Orange tubular flowers appear occasionally on mature clumps in spring. Water only when the soil has dried out and keep bone-dry through winter, since it is markedly more cold-sensitive than many landscape aloes.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; strong sun and lean feeding intensify the signature brick-red foliage color of Cameron's aloe.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply draining soil in full sun, since bright exposure and minimal supplemental fertility are what deepen this Zimbabwean species' foliage color. Slender, recurved leaves shift from green to a striking brick-red to coppery-maroon through the cooler, drier months, an effect that intensifies with stress from sun and dry soil and fades toward green with shade or lush growing conditions. Clustering rosettes spread steadily by offsets to form a dense, colorful groundcover, and branched spikes of coral-red tubular flowers open in winter above the foliage. Water only sparingly once established and avoid rich soil or heavy feeding, which promotes green growth at the expense of the prized red coloration.

common_name: Rooikappie Aloe (Little Red Riding Hood Hybrid Aloe)

planting.note: Plant offsets or nursery divisions in spring in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; Rooikappie is a compact South African hybrid valued for its nearly year-round bloom.

directions: Grow in lean, sharply draining soil in full sun, where compact rosettes of narrow, gray-green, faintly spotted leaves cluster and offset freely to form a tidy, spreading clump. Named for the vivid orange-red flower spikes that top the plant almost continuously through the seasons where the climate stays mild, Rooikappie is prized among landscape aloes for blooming far more often than most of its relatives, attracting sunbirds and hummingbirds whenever flowers are present. Its compact size and long bloom season make it well suited to borders, rock gardens, and containers in a xeriscape planting. Water only occasionally once established, letting soil dry between waterings, and remove spent flower spikes to keep new ones coming.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
